blocks.text: Fruit of the buṭm tree: kḍāma (Musil [=Alois Musil, Arabia Petraea III] 3, 152). Terebinth nuts, bizr el-buṭm, yield an edible oil (Mielck [=?] 16).

Jews: Bacher, Tanchum [=Wilhelm Bacher, Aus dem Wörterbuche Tanchum Jeruschalmi's] 43 for boṭnīm. Physicians: Sha [=M. Steinschneider, Heilmittelnamen der Araber] 292. Berggren ms. [=Berggren manuscript of the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft]: boṭm = شجر الترمنتين [shajar al-turmantīn] Mowat, Alphita [=J. L. G. Mowat (ed.), Alphita: A Medico-Botanical Glossary] 5 albotm.

The Syrians, besides boṭm, also الحبّة الخضراء [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ] (Sha 562) BA. [=Bar ʿAlī, Syriac-Arabic lexicon] 2354. BB. [=Bar Bahlūl, Lexicon syriacum] 274. 381. 829. Guigues [=P. Guigues, Le livre de l'art du Traitement de Najim Ad-Dyn Mahmoud] 39. Likewise Kroner, Maim. [=Hermann Kroner, edition of a medical treatise of Maimonides] passim, with the ital. [=Italian] translation זרע אטרבנטינא for it.

A small evergreen tree or shrub. As a component of evergreen maquis it is certainly endemic throughout the entire Mediterranean region, from Syria and Eretz Yisrael to the Canary Islands, and also in North Africa (Hehn [=Victor Hehn, Kulturpflanzen und Haustiere] 429). Illustration in Vietz [=Ferdinand Bernhard Vietz, Icones plantarum medico-oeconomico-technologicarum] 2, 11. In 1804 Vietz still praises the medicinal effects of mastic resin, whereas it is now officinal only in Austria (Strassburger ^{15} [=Strasburger, Lehrbuch der Botanik, 15th ed.] 577). Bloch [=Samson Bloch, Sĕbīlē ʿōlam] 2, 82, probably the first among Jews, describes the tree and its resin. Modern Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew: האלה קשת העלים = سريس [sarīs] (Hasade [=Hasade, Hebrew agricultural monthly] 1, 3, 32). Inexactly בטנים**) (3, 454. 4, 312), erroneously שיח הלוט (6, 206).

The tree also yields mastic (Haynald, Mézgák [=Lajos Haynald, A szentírási mézgák és gyanták termőnövényei] 14. 28) in Eretz Yisrael (P. [=George E. Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] 207), but for commerce it has for a long time (Benjamin v. [=of] Tudela, p. [=page] 20 of the Grünhutschen Übersetzung [=L. Grünhut, Die Reisebeschreibungen des R. Benjamin von Tudela]) been obtained only on the island of Chios from a cultivated variety (Moeller ^{2} [=Joseph Moeller, Lehrbuch der Pharmakognosie, 2nd ed.] 431). The annual production averages 125,000 kg [=kilograms]. Josua Benveniste [=Joshua Benveniste, Śĕde Jĕhōšuaʿ], rabbi in Constantinople, reports in his commentary on jḤalla [=Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Ḥalla] 4, 9 f. [=folio] 177^{d}, published in 1662, that in the Turkish empire mastic may be produced only on the island of Chios (כיאו). Already Benjamin of Tudela has nothing more to report about the island of Chios (כיא) than that 400 Jews live there and that the tree from which mastic מצטיקי is collected is found there (1, 25 Asher. [=A. Asher, The Itinerary of Rabbi Benjamin of Tudela]).

In the Middle Ages mastic was regarded as a remedy; today it is used for varnishes and putties. In the Orient it has been in use as a chewing resin since ancient times, and that of Eretz Yisrael was considered the best according to the testimony of Plinius [=Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia] (Killermann [=Sebastian Killermann, Die Blumen des heiligen Landes] 1, 34). Plin. 14, 25 says: in oriente optimam tenuissimamque [resinam] terebinthi fundunt, dein lentisci, quam et masticen vocant. Naḥmani [=Moses ben Naḥman (Nahmanides), Commentary on the Pentateuch] knows

The wild pistachio “P. Lent.” on the mountains of Judah ZDPV. [=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins] 8, 104, on Tabor 107, in the Carmel woodlands, will be the terebinth. Terebinth and pistachio are not distinguished in Ritter [=Carl Ritter, Erdkunde von Asien] (14 index sv. [=sub voce] buttom).

Bodenheimer [=F. S. Bodenheimer, Kĕnīmat hamāgēn], kĕnīmōt hamāgēn, Tel-Aviv 1924, p. 32. 41 f. [=and the following] erroneously: bŏṭnīm = P. Lentiscus L., ʾēlā P. mutica Fisch. et Mey. [=Fischer et Meyer] P. Tereb. u. [=and] P. vera.
